stem: Defence mechanisms in operation Sublimation Identify the defence mechanism used in each of the following situations: Reaction formation Dissociation A boy who is being bullied at school takes on the identity of Superman. Suppression Intellectualization A woman is not able to recall the abuse she sustained as a child. Regression An idle woman who is not performing well at her job is fired. She states this is because her colleague is bad- Rationalisation mouthing her rather than admitting her poor performance. Repression Denial A man who was diagnosed to have cancer says, "This cannot be true... I follow a healthy lifestyle."
correctAnswer: A boy who is being bullied at school takes on the identity of Superman. → Reaction formation, A woman is not able to recall the abuse she sustained as a child. → Repression, An idle woman who is not performing well at her job is fired. She states this is because her colleague is bad-mouthing her rather than admitting her poor performance. → Rationalization, A man who was diagnosed to have cancer says, "This cannot be true... I follow a healthy lifestyle." → Denial
explanation: Reaction formation is the management of unacceptable impulses by permitting expression of the impulse in antithetical form. Repression is characterised by preventing unacceptable aspects of internal reality from coming to conscious attention. (For example, a victim of childhood abuse may not have conscious awareness of the abuse as an adult.) The associated emotional reaction may remain in the conscious mind but divorced from its accompanying memory. Rationalisation involves finding excuses that will justify unacceptable behaviours when self-esteem is threatened. Denial is defined as the expressed refusal to recognise a threatening reality. It is of relevance especially to those with serious physical illnesses, where the patient denies being told of the presence of illness in themselves or their loved ones. It may persist despite constant reiteration of the facts.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1067. Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 892. Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4 th Edition. 2019. pp. 129-130.

Mitmachen is a motor symptom of catatonia where the patient’s limbs can be moved without resistance to any position. The limbs return to their resting state once the examiner lets go, in contrast with catalepsy where the limbs remain in their set positions for prolonged periods. Mitgehen is an extreme form of mitmachen where the patient’s limbs can be moved to any position by very slight or fingertip pressure. Gegenhalten is when an individual with catatonia opposes all passive movements with the same degree of force as that which is being applied by the examiner. Ambitendency is a motor symptom of catatonia in which there is an alternating mixture of automatic obedience and negativism. Cataplexy is a symptom of narcolepsy in which there is sudden loss of muscle tone, leading to collapse. This usually occurs following emotional stress.

Waxy flexibility (also known as catalepsy or flexibilitas cerea) is a rare motor symptom of catatonia that describes a situation in which the patient’s limbs can be passively moved to any posture, which will then be held for a prolonged period of time.

Substance P Alzheimer's disease Circadian function disorders Neurotensin Schizophrenia Migraine Neuropeptide Y Depression OCD Corticotropin-releasing factor Huntington's disease Endocannabinoids Parkinson's disease Feeding
correctAnswer: Substance P → Huntington's disease, Neurotensin → Schizophrenia, Neuropeptide Y → Feeding, Corticotropin- releasing factor → Depression, Endocannabinoids → Schizophrenia
explanation: Substance P is the primary neurotransmitter in most primary afferent sensory neurons (Pain) and is also seen in the striatonigral pathway. Levels of substance P have been reported to be markedly reduced in patients with Huntington's chorea. Neurotensin coexists with dopamine in some axon terminals. Neurotensin-related peptides are being investigated in the treatment of psychotic symptoms. Neuropeptide Y may play an important role in feeding disorders through its effects on energy balance. It is secreted by the hypothalamus and in addition to increasing food intake, it increases the proportion of energy stored as fat and blocks nociceptive signals to the brain. Corticotropin releasing factor (CRF) is the neurotransmitter associated with anxiety and depression, and CRF receptor antagonists are currently under clinical evaluation as anxiolytics and antidepressants. The endocannabinoids are associated with schizophrenia and psychotic disorders. Anandamide (weak ligand) and 2-arachnidonylglycerol (strong) are formed from arachidonic acid and ethanolamine - belong to endocannabinoid family. The two types of cannabinoid receptors, central (CB1) and peripheral (CB2), bind tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the active ingredient of marijuana. CB1 receptors are found in the brain and are potential targets for the treatment of both pain and psychosis. CB2 receptors are associated with immune regulation.

Intelligence is correlated to the load of chromosomal damage
correctAnswer: Intelligence is correlated to the load of chromosomal damage
explanation: Fragile X syndrome (FXS) is the most common single gene disorder, which causes autism and intellectual disability. The fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene is silenced when CGG Triplet repeats exceed 200, which is the full mutation that causes FXS. Carriers of FXS have a CGG repeat of between 55 and 200, which is defined as a premutation and transcription of the gene is overactive with high levels of the FMR1 mRNA. Most carriers of the premutation have normal levels of fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP) and a normal intelligence, but in the upper range of the premutation (120-200) the FMRP level may be lower than normal. The clinical problems associated with the premutation are caused by the RNA toxicity associated with increased FMR1mRNA levels, although for some mildly lowered FMRP can cause problems associated with FXS.

stem: Which of the following enzymes is responsible for the degradation of noradrenaline?
explanation: Norepinephrine (NE) action is terminated by two principal destructive or catabolic enzymes that turn NE into inactive metabolites. stem: Which of the following substance is the most active ingredient in the Ethiopian plant Catha edulis, whose leaves on chewing provide amphetamine-like stimulation?
explanation: Catha edulis, or ‘Khat’, is a plant indigenous to Eastern Africa and Southern Arabia. It releases a variety of psychoactive chemicals, including the stimulants cathinone and cathine. Khat is chewed like tobacco and held between the cheek and gums after chewing. The stimulant effect of the Khat plant was originally attributed to cathine, but this was disputed by reports showing the plant extracts from fresh leaves contained another substance more active than cathine - called cathinone. Cathinone is not very stable and breaks down to produce cathine and norephedrine. This explains why fresh leaves are more stimulating, and the habit of chewing Khat is more or less confined to the regions where it is cultivated. In the mid-2000s, synthetic cathinones began to appear, marketed as ‘legal high’ chemicals. They were packaged under labels including ‘screen cleaner’, ‘jewelry cleaner’, and most notoriously ‘bath salts’. These compounds are substituted cathinones that are chemically modified to avoid regulatory control. Generally, substituted cathinones increase synaptic catecholamine levels by inhibiting the dopamine, serotonin, and norepinephrine reuptake transporters in a fashion similar to cocaine. Most also facilitate catecholamine release, similar to methamphetamine.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 303.

stem: The receptors which have both pre and postsynaptic presence are
explanation: Dopamine receptors are divided into two groups. The first group is the D1-like receptors, including both D1 and D5 receptors. D1-like receptors are excitatory, and positively linked to adenylate cyclase. The second group is the D2-like receptors, including D2, D3, and D4 receptors. D2-like receptors are inhibitory and negatively linked to adenylate cyclase. Thus, the neurotransmitter DA can be either excitatory or inhibitory, depending on which DA receptor it binds. All five DA receptors can be located postsynaptically, but D2 and D3 receptors can also both be located presynaptically, where, due to their inhibitory actions, they act as autoreceptors to inhibit further DA release.
reference: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5 th Edition. 2021. pp. 81-82.

stem: Which of the following is the most powerful endogenous opioid peptide?
explanation: Dynorphin A has been described as ‘extraordinarily potent’ (‘dyn from the Greek, dynamis = power and ‘orphin’ for the endogenous morphine peptide). Dynorphin peptides are released in the brain during stress exposure. After they are released, they activate kappa opioid receptors distributed throughout the brain and spinal cord, where they trigger cellular responses resulting in different stress responses: analgesia, dysphoria-like behaviours, anxiety-like responses, and increased addiction behaviours in experimental animals.
reference: Chavkin C. Dynorphin–still an extraordinarily potent opioid peptide. Molecular pharmacology. 2013 Apr 1;83(4):729-36.

stem: All of the following intrauterine infections cause intellectual disabilities except
explanation: Maternal infections during pregnancy, especially viral infections, have been known to cause fetal damage and intellectual disability. Syphilis (caused by Treponema pallidum) in pregnant women was once the leading cause of various neuropathic changes in their offspring, including intellectual disability. Rubella (German measles) has now replaced syphilis as the primary cause of congenital malformations and intellectual disability caused by maternal infection. Children with intellectual disability from cytomegalovirus frequently have cerebral calcification, microcephaly, or hydrocephalus. Toxoplasmosis causes mild to severe intellectual disability and, in severe cases, hydrocephalus, seizures, microcephaly, and chorioretinitis. EBV (Infectious Mononucleosis) has not been implicated in intellectual disability syndromes.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 104.

stem: Which of the following is least likely to occur in schizophrenia?
explanation: Macroscopic brain changes that occur in schizophrenia include enlarged ventricle size and reductions in grey matter volume, whole-brain volume, and white matter anisotropy. The reduced neuropil (intertwined axons and dendrites of neurons) hypothesis has been suggested as a microanatomical explanation to account for these macroscopic changes. Studies have found both increased and decreased neuronal density in the cerebral cortex. The literature provides support for increased neuron density in schizophrenia, with variation dependent on age. Although the brain is abnormal, gliosis is absent.
reference: Bakhshi K, Chance SA. The neuropathology of schizophrenia: a selective review of past studies and emerging themes in brain structure and cytoarchitecture. Neuroscience. 2015 Sep 10;303:82-102. Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 189.

stem: An intravenous heroin user presents with significant slowing of cognitive ability. He has fatuous affect and impaired concentration that has developed insidiously. Which of the following is a likely diagnosis?
explanation: HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND) is an umbrella term for the spectrum of neurocognitive impairment induced by HIV (direct effects of HIV). It ranges from asymptomatic impairment to severe impairment with pronounced deficits in self-efficacy and interference with day-to-day activities. Early indicators of HAND include impairments in psychomotor function, in simple and divided attention and concentration, in mental agility, and in mental flexibility. HAND also relates to personality changes (e.g. apathy, irritability, and inertia) and changes in behaviour (e.g. social withdrawal and impaired activities of daily living). Neurological signs of HAND include poor concentration, loss of balance, and tremor.
reference: Knights MJ et al. HIV infection and its psychiatric manifestations: a clinical overview. BJPsych Advances. 2017 Jul;23(4):265-77 Taylor DM, Gaughran F, Pillinger T. The Maudsley Practice Guidelines for Physical Health Conditions in Psychiatry. 2021.

stem: A 58 year old man presents with postural hypotension, anorexia, nausea and weakness. He appears to be extremely apathetic, with significant anhedonia compounded by fatigue and depressed mood.Which of the following hormonal imbalance is most likely?
explanation: Addison syndrome may result from adrenal destruction by autoimmune disease, metastatic cancer, tuberculosis, or human immunodeficiency virus infection or secondary to suppression of ACTH secretion by chronic corticosteroid therapy. Addison disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) is characterised by chronic glucocorticoid and/or mineralocorticoid deficiency due to failure of the adrenal cortex. It should be suspected in all acutely or chronically ill patients with general fatigue or severe weakness and unexplained dehydration, hypotension, weight loss, fever, abdominal pain, and hyperpigmentation. Psychiatric symptoms include apathy, anhedonia, fatigue, and depressed mood. It may be misdiagnosed as major depressive disorder. Anorexia is common in both depression and Addison disease, but the presence of nausea, vomiting and hyperpigmentation may suggest Addison disease.
reference: Barthel A et al. An update on Addison’s disease. Experimental and Clinical Endocrinology & Diabetes. 2019 Feb;127(02/03):165-75.

stem: Choose the antidepressant which, if given to a pregnant mother, is most likely to cause withdrawal symptoms in the neonate?
explanation: When antidepressants are taken during pregnancy, the neonate may experience discontinuation symptoms, which are usually mild, such as agitation and irritability, or rarely respiratory distress and convulsions (with SSRIs). The risk is assumed to be particularly high with short half- life drugs such as paroxetine and venlafaxine. Continuing to breastfeed and then ‘weaning’ by switching to mixed (breast/bottle) feeding may help reduce the severity of reactions.

stem: The drug that is most likely to result in a hypertensive crisis from the given list is
explanation: The most worrisome side effect of MAOIs (such as phenelzine) is the tyramine-induced hypertensive crisis (‘cheese reaction’). The amino acid tyramine is normally transformed via GI metabolism. However, MAOIs inactivate GI metabolism of dietary tyramine, thus allowing intact tyramine to enter the circulation. A hypertensive crisis may subsequently occur because of a powerful pressor effect of the amino acid.

stem: Which of the following is not a significant risk factor for the development of antidepressant induced SIADH?
explanation: Most antidepressants have been associated with hyponatraemia. It has been suggested that serotonergic drugs are relatively more likely than noradrenergic drugs to cause hypnonatraemia, although this is disputed. Risk factors include: older age (most important), female sex, major surgery, history of hyponatraemia or a low baseline sodium concentration, co-therapy with other drugs known to be associated hyponatraemia (e.g. diuretics, NSAIDs, antipsychotics, carbamazepine, cancer chemotherapy, calcium antagonists, ACE inhibitors, and laxatives), reduced renal function, medical co-morbidity (e.g. hypothyroidism, diabetes, COPD, hypertension, head injury, congestive cardiac failure, cerebrovascular accident, various cancers), and low body weight.

stem: Which of the following has been associated with the use of SSRIs in mid-late pregnancy?
explanation: A specific problem that has been associated with serotonergic antidepressant use in mid to late pregnancy is persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN). Although initial reports suggested an approximate six-fold increase, recent literature has shown the absolute risk to be small and more modest. Although the risk of PPHN in babies exposed in utero to SSRIs is increased, the absolute risk is low.

explanation: Deaths from neuroleptic malignant syndrome are usually due to respiratory failure, cardiovascular collapse, myoglobinuric renal failure, sepsis, arrythmias, thromboembolism, or disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).

explanation: The relative liability of individual antipsychotic medications for akathisia is uncertain, but there is consensus that the incidence is lowest for olanzapine, quetiapine, and clozapine. stem: Mr.X is a 33 year old gentleman with a long standing diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia. He was started on atypical anti psychotic medication 6 months ago and when reviewed in the clinic, he complains of side effects such as reduced sexual function and has also developed enlarged breasts. Which of the following anti psychotic drugs is most likely to be associated with these side effects?
explanation: When D2 antagonists are administered, D2 receptors in the tuberoinfundibular dopamine pathway are blocked. This causes plasma prolactin concentrations to rise, a condition called hyperprolactinaemia. This can be associated with galactorrhea (i.e. breast secretions), sexual dysfunction, gynaecomastia (enlargement of the breasts) in men, and amenorrhea (i.e. irregular or lack of menstrual periods) in women.

stem: Zolpidem acts as an agonist at
explanation: Z drugs bind to benzodiazepine-sensitive GABA-A receptors. A different nomenclature (omega system) denotes the specific sites of GABA-A receptors where these ‘Z’ drugs act as omega-1 receptors. Conventional benzodiazepines interact at both ω1 and ω2 sites, the latter likely contributing to side effects. Zolpidem and zaleplon bind selectively to alpha-1 subunits of these sites. By contrast, benzodiazepines, zopiclone and eszopiclone bind to four alpha subunits (alpha-1, alpha-2, alpha-3, and alpha-5). The functional significance of alpha-1 selectivity is not yet proven, but may contribute to lower risk of tolerance and dependence. The alpha-1 subtype is known to be critical for producing sedation and thus is targeted by every effective GABA-A PAM (positive allosteric modulator) hypnotic, both benzodiazepines and Z-drugs.
reference: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5 th Edition. 2021. pp. 422-423. Madari S, Golebiowski R, Mansukhani MP, Kolla BP. Pharmacological management of insomnia. Neurotherapeutics. 2021 Jan;18(1):44-52.

stem: Which of the following medications is not associated with an increased risk of depression?
explanation: Orlistat interferes with the absorption of dietary fats, causing reduced caloric intake. It works by inhibiting gastric and pancreatic lipases, the enzymes that break down triglycerides in the intestine. The most common subjective side effects of orlistat are GI related and include steatorrhea, flatulence, fecal incontinence, and frequent or urgent bowel movements. Hepatic and renal injuries are potentially severe side effects or orlistat use. It has not been associated with an increased risk of depression.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 708-709.

explanation: Paroxetine has the highest anticholinergic effects of the SSRIs. Paroxetine’s mild anticholinergic actions can enhance the rapid onset of anxiolytic and hypnotic efficacy, but also cause mild anticholinergic side effects.

stem: Which combination could be prescribed together, in which the second drug is used to minimize the adverse effect of the first one?
explanation: Reboxetine is a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor. Side effects may appear ‘anticholinergic’, but reboxetine does not directly block muscarinic receptors. Constipation, dry mouth, and urinary retention are noradrenergic, due in part to peripheral alpha 1 receptor stimulation causing decreased acetylcholine release. Thus, antidotes for these side effects can be alpha 1 antagonists such as tamsulosin or doxazosin, especially in men over 50 with borderline urine flow.

stem: What happens to GABA-A receptors in benzodiazepine withdrawal state?
options: Reduced inhibitory tone in the CNS
explanation: Chronic benzodiazepine administration may lead to uncoupling of the linkage between GABAA and benzodiazepine receptor sites and subsequent preferential degradation of certain GABAA receptor units. Such a change results in a long-term homeostatic adaptation to the chronic presence of benzodiazepines leading to a reduction in GABA receptor density. Sudden withdrawal of the benzodiazepine once tolerance has developed would expose the recipient to underactive GABA system without the counterbalancing presence of benzodiazepine drugs.

explanation: Shorter-acting benzodiazepines (e.g. oxazepam) may be preferred in those for whom over-sedation must be avoided, in people with liver disease who may not be able to metabolise long-acting agents efficiently, and in people with COPD. stem: Which one among the following is more related to causing discontinuation syndrome?
explanation: Discontinuation effects can be more common or more severe with paroxetine than with other SSRIs. Paroxetine’s discontinuation effects may be related to the fact that it inhibits its own metabolism. Thus, when paroxetine is withdrawn, the rate of its decline can be faster as it stops inhibiting its metabolism. Readaptation of cholinergic receptors after prolonged blockade may also contribute to the discontinuation effects of paroxetine.

stem: Which of the following is correct with regard to the pharmacokinetics of depot antipsychotics?
options: Test doses are not useful to avoid severe adverse effects
Higher doses are significantly more effective than lower doses
Adverse effects are usually short lived than oral medications due to the low frequency of administration
Plasma level of depot antipsychotics could be as high as 4 times the initial levels, 2 to 3 months after starting treatment
Shortening the dosing intervals can improve efficacy in non-responders
correctAnswer: Plasma level of depot antipsychotics could be as high as 4 times the initial levels, 2 to 3 months after starting treatment
explanation: For first-generation antipsychotic (FGA) depots, a test dose should be given. Because of its long half-life, any adverse effects from the administration of a depot are likely to be long-lived. For FGAs, a test dose consisting of a small dose of active drug in a small volume of oil serves a dual purpose: it is a test of the patient’s sensitivity to EPS and of any sensitivity to the base oil. For second-generation antipsychotic (SGA) depots, test doses may not be required (less propensity to cause EPS and aqueous base not known to be allergenic) although they could be considered appropriate where a patient is suspected of being non-adherent to oral antipsychotic medication and the depot will be the first exposure to guaranteed antipsychotic medication delivery. For both types of depots, prior treatment with the equivalent oral formulation is preferred to assess efficacy and tolerability. At the start of therapy, plasma drug levels increase over several weeks to months without increasing the given dose. (This is due to accumulation: steady state is only achieved after at least 6-8 weeks.) There are few data showing clear dose-response effects for depots. There is some information indicating that low doses (within the licensed range) may be at least as effective as higher ones. Depots should be administered at the longest possible licensed interval. There is no evidence to suggest that shortening the dose interval improves efficacy.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 67-68.

stem: Which of the following is the most important property of a depot antipsychotic medication?
options: The elimination is almost entirely renal
explanation: Depot antipsychotics are esters formed between the alcohol group of the antipsychotic compound and a long chain of fatty acids (enantic, decanoic, palmitic, and undecylenic acid), and this ester is dissolved in oil (sesame oil or Viscoleo). Antipsychotic compounds are generally fat-soluble, but the esterification increases this fat solubility 1000 times (the longer the carbon chain of the fatty acid esters, the more the fat solubility). The ester is released from the oil phase by slow diffusion into the body water phase. The higher the fat solubility, the slower the release. (Kane et al., European Neuropsychopharmacology 1998, 8: 55-56)

stem: Mrs. P suffers from bipolar disorder and is on lithium carbonate treatment. She also suffers from systemic hypertension. The ideal drug of choice for treating her hypertension would be
explanation: ACE inhibitors (e.g. captopril, ramipril) can reduce thirst (which can lead to mild dehydration) and increase renal sodium loss (leading to increased sodium re-absorption by the kidney), resulting in an increase in lithium plasma levels. The magnitude of this effect is variable, from no increase to a four-fold increase. Care is also required with angiotensin II receptor antagonists such as candesartan. Diuretics can reduce the renal clearance of lithium, the magnitude of this effect being greater with thiazide than loop diuretics. Lithium levels usually rise within 10 days of a thiazide diuretic (e.g. bendroflumethiazide, chlortalidone, inadapamide, xipamide) being prescribed. Beta-blockers like propranalol are relatively safe to be used with lithium.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 252-253.

stem: Pharmacokinetic properties of SSRIs include all except
options: Presence of active metabolite with longer half life for certain compounds
Requirement for a washout period prior to administration of an MAOI
Non linear elimination kinetics in high doses
explanation: SSRIs are well, but not rapidly, absorbed after oral administration. They have their peak effects in the range of 3-8 hours. Absorption of sertraline may be slightly enhanced by food. All SSRIs have a long half-life, which allows once daily administration. Fluoxetine has the most prolonged half-life: 4-6 days; its active metabolite has a half-life of 7-9 days. The half-life of sertraline is 26 hours, and its less active metabolite has a half-life of 3-5 days. Fluoxetine displays non-linear kinetics probably owing to the saturation of liver enzymes. Higher doses can result in disproportionately higher plasma levels.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 625.

stem: Choose the correct option regarding effects of smoking?
explanation: Tobacco smoke contains polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons that induce (increase the activity of) certain hepatic enzymes (CYP1A2 in particular). The extent of enzyme induction is determined by the number and type of cigarettes smoked and the degree of smoke inhalation. For some drugs used in psychiatry, smoking significantly reduces drug plasma levels and higher doses are required than in non-smokers. Smoking reduces plasma clozapine levels by up to 50%.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 856.

stem: A child attains gender identity in which stage of Freud's psychosexual development?
explanation: The phallic stage begins sometime during year 3 and continues until approximately the end of year 5. The phallic stage lays the foundation for gender identity and serves to integrate residues from the previous stages into a predominantly genital-sexual orientation.

stem: In your CAMHS clinic, you observe Mollie, a five-year-old girl, as she plays with her doll. You notice that she is talking to her doll as though it is real. What is the name of this phenomenon?
explanation: Animism is the belief that plants, inanimate objects and natural phenomena possess a living soul and have human-like feelings and intentions. In Piaget’s pre-operational stage, children use such animistic thinking to endow physical events and objects with life-like psychological attributes, such as feelings and intentions.

stem: According to Kohlberg, which one among the following represent Conventional Stage?
explanation: Lawrence Kohlberg integrated Jean Piaget’s concepts and described multiple stages of moral development within three significant levels of morality. The first level is pre-conventional morality, in which punishment and obedience are the determining factors. The second level is morality of conventional role-conformity, in which children try to conform to gain approval and maintain good relationships with others and are also guided by rigid codes of ‘law and order’ (authority orientation). The third and highest level is the morality of self-accepted moral principles (post-conventional), in which children voluntarily comply with rules based on a concept of universal ethical principles and make exceptions to rules in certain circumstances.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 902. Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4 th Edition. 2015.

correctAnswer: Primacy effect is related to initial items receiving most consolidation
explanation: In serial learning, the primacy effect is a tendency for the items near the beginning of the series to be better recalled than those near the middle. stem: Which of the following can reduce groupthink?
explanation: Groupthink is a collective pattern of defensive avoidance, characteristic of group decision making in organisations in which group members develop rationalisations supporting shared illusions of their own infallibility and invulnerability with the organisation. Characteristic features include: an illusion of invulnerability, collective efforts to rationalise in order to discount warnings, an unquestioned belief in the group’s inherent morality, stereotyped views of rivals and enemies, direct pressure on any member who dissents from the consensus view, self- censorship of disagreements with the apparent group consensus, a shared illusion of unanimity, and the emergence of self-appointed protectors of the group from adverse information that might undermine the existing complacency. Various strategies that can reduce groupthink include appointing a 'devil's advocate', encouraging open debate, acknowledging the presence of groupthink, seeking external opinion, splitting the group into smaller units for discussion, holding last chance meetings to encourage challenges, and reserving leaders' opinions until after the group's discussion has been completed.

stem: The ethics to determine goodness from acts and intentions behind them rather than their consequences is
explanation: According to Immanuel Kant, a German philosopher, deontology is an ethical approach centered on rules and professional duties. Unlike many ethical theories, deontology does not focus on the consequences of individual actions. Personal emotions behind actions also do not matter with Kantian deontology because Kant believed humans do not always have rational control over their feelings. Instead, the intent behind chosen actions holds far more importance. Therefore, deontology proponents judge actions based on what people consider to be morally correct, regardless of actual consequences. Consequentialist moral theories are teleological: they aim at some goal state and evaluate the morality of actions in terms of progress toward that state. The best-known version of consequentialism is utilitarianism. As most clearly stated by Mill a proponent of the utilitarianism (teleology), the basic principle of utilitarianism is: Actions are right to the degree that they tend to promote the greatest good for the greatest number.

Accordingly, rights and duties determine action and so it is also called as absolutism. The term Teleology derives its name from the Greek 'Teleon', meaning 'purpose' and the central concept is that rather than rights, people have interests, whether these are concerns, desires or needs. explanation: Elevated plasma total homocysteine is a modifiable risk factor for development of cognitive decline, dementia, and Alzheimer’s disease in older persons. In a variety of clinical studies, the relative risk of dementia in elderly people for moderately raised homocysteine ranges from 1.1.5 to 2.5, and the Population Attributable risk ranges from 4.3 to 31%. Intervention trials in elderly with cognitive impairment show that homocysteine-lowering treatment with B vitamins markedly slows the rate of whole and regional brain atrophy and also slows cognitive decline. Initially, neurological changes such as anxiety, poor concentration, fatigue, and depression can manifest (due to reduced serotonin synthesis), but as pellagra advances, dementia and delirium may occur. stem: Capgras syndrome (l'illusion des soies) is:
options: Also called the phantom mirror image
explanation: Capgras syndrome (l’illusion des sosies) is a type of delusional misidentification in which the patient believes that a person known to them has been replaced by a ‘double’ who is to all external appearances identical but is not the ‘real person’.

stem: A 20-year-old man is unable to express his problem coherently but appears very confused and feels that 'something is happening but not sure what it is'. This sense of perplexity and uncertainty that exists during a prodrome of psychosis may be linked most appropriately to which of the following experiences?
explanation: Delusional mood is recalled as arising following a period when there is an abnormal mood state characterised by anticipatory anxiety, a sense of ‘something is about to happen’ and an increased sense of the significance of minor events. stem: A 43-year-old woman, who was involved in a serious flight accident, felt at the time of the accident as if she had become unreal. For some time, she felt as if something had changed and that she was not herself. This is known as:
explanation: Depersonalisation is an unpleasant subjective experience where the patient feels as if they have become ‘unreal’. It is a feeling that one is not oneself or that something has changed. Often this is associated with a feeling of unreality, so that the environment is experienced as flat, dull, and unreal (known as ‘derealisation’). Many people who complain of depersonalisation also state that their capacity for feeling is diminished or absent. This is a subjective experience because to the outside observer there is no loss of ability to respond emotionally and appropriately to any given situation. Depersonalisation is not a delusion, and it should be distinguished from nihilistic delusions in which the patient denies that they exist or that they are alive, or that the work or other people exist. Depersonalisation is a non-specific symptom occurring in many psychiatric disorders, as well as in ‘normal’ people.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 108. Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 10. th Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4 Edition. 2019. pp. 81-82.

stem: Of various thought disorders classified by Andreasen, which of the following are more common in schizophrenia than mania?
explanation: Nancy Andreasen created a scale in which the classic formal thought disorders are subdivided into three groups: Communication disturbances: when the speaker does not meet the necessary requirements for the listener’s understanding (poverty of content of speech, pressure of speech, distractible speech, tangentiality, derailment, stilted speech, echolalia, self-reference, circumstantiality, loss of goal, perseveration, and blocking) Language disturbances: when the speaker violates the semantic and syntactic conventions (incoherence, clang association, neologisms, use of word approximations) Thought disturbances: when only thinking alone seems affected (poverty of thought and illogically aberrant inferential processes) Andreasen demonstrated that these psychopathological findings were not specific to schizophrenia and were also common in other mental disorders (e.g. mania). Of those listed, derailment (synonymous with loose associations - a symptom of schizophrenic thought disorder in which there is a total break in the chain of association between the meaning of thoughts) is more common in schizophrenia than mania.
reference:
Jerónimo J et al. Formal Thought Disorders–Historical Roots. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2018 Nov 9;9:572. Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 108.

explanation: Dysmegalopsia refers to a change in the perceived shape of an object. explanation: Echolalia is the repetition of phrases or sentences spoken by others (e.g., the examiner). It is an echophenomenon that may be seen in catatonia. Other echophenomena are echopraxia (repeating what you do) and mirror movements (doing as you do at the same time).

stem: The nature of speech produced in Broca aphasia is
options: Effortful but with grammatical use of language
explanation: Broca aphasia (also called non-fluent or expressive aphasia) had traditionally been characterised by non-fluent speech and impaired repetition but intact auditory comprehension. It has long been thought to be associated with damage to Broca area (i.e. left inferior frontal convolution) or Brodmann area 44. Broca aphasia is characterised by retained use of nouns and verbs, but the patient may have lost all forms of pronouns, articles, and conjunctions, and hence may struggle to speak more than one word at a time even with enormous effort.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 48.

stem: Mr X was admitted to the psychiatric unit with a history of elated mood, overactivity, restlessness, grandiose delusions, disinhibited behaviour and was diagnosed with mania. A student nurse observed that he also experienced third person auditory hallucinations and wondered whether first rank symptoms could occur in manic patients. He wanted to clarify this with the treating psychiatric doctor in the team. Choose the most appropriate statement from the following:
options: First rank symptoms never occur in manic patients
First rank symptoms may present in 10-25% of manic patients
First rank symptoms are very rarely seen in manic patients
First rank symptoms are present in all cases of mania with psychosis
First rank symptoms are present in nearly half of all patients with mania
correctAnswer: First rank symptoms may present in 10-25% of manic patients
explanation: First rank symptoms are a group of symptoms that have special significance in the diagnosis of schizophrenia. They are useful because they occur reasonably often in schizophrenia and more rarely in other disorders, and it is not too difficult to tell whether they are present or not. However, there is no symptom that is pathognomonic of schizophrenia. First rank symptoms can all be reported in other conditions (e.g. organic psychoses, manic illnesses). First rank symptoms are present in approximately 10-30% of patients with mania.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 110. Channa A et al. First rank symptoms in Mania: An indistinct diagnostic strand. Acta Medica International. 2016 Jul 1;3(2):20.

stem: Compulsory treatment cannot be justified under which of the following ethical principles?
explanation: A fundamental principle of medical care is that treatment of a patient should be with their consent. A patient has a right to decide for themselves which treatments to undergo and which treatments to refuse (autonomy). This right is retained, even when the refusal of treatment could result in death or significant deterioration in health. Treatment without consent is possible only in certain circumstances, constrained by appropriate laws.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 936.
